results.name: pow2_vs_other_even_contrast
results.description: For sets whose examples are all powers of two (e.g. 16,32,2,8; 2,8; 8,64; 64,4), yes rate on non-example powers of two minus yes rate on other even targets; observed above null_mean means people restrict to the small nested rule more sharply than the model (model over-generalizes to the larger "even"/multiples rules), below means the model is too sharp.
results.code:
# name: pow2_vs_other_even_contrast
# description: For sets whose examples are all powers of two (e.g. 16,32,2,8; 2,8; 8,64; 64,4), yes rate on non-example powers of two minus yes rate on other even targets; observed above null_mean means people restrict to the small nested rule more sharply than the model (model over-generalizes to the larger "even"/multiples rules), below means the model is too sharp.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    pow2 = np.array([2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64], dtype=float)
    isp = np.isin(ex, pow2) | np.isnan(ex)
    all_p = isp.all(axis=1) & ~np.isnan(ex).all(axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    is_ex = (ex == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    tp = np.isin(t, pow2)
    a = all_p & ~is_ex & tp
    b = all_p & ~is_ex & ~tp & (t % 2 == 0)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: lag1_residual_autocorr
results.description: Lag-1 correlation of consecutive within-session residuals (rating minus number_set mean rating), sessions split where trial_index does not increase by 1; observed above null_mean means people perseverate on their previous answer beyond what the stimuli explain (model lacks sequential dependence).
results.code:
# name: lag1_residual_autocorr
# description: Lag-1 correlation of consecutive within-session residuals (rating minus number_set mean rating), sessions split where trial_index does not increase by 1; observed above null_mean means people perseverate on their previous answer beyond what the stimuli explain (model lacks sequential dependence).
def test_statistic(df):
    r = df["rating"].astype(float)
    res = (r - r.groupby(df["number_set"]).transform("mean")).to_numpy()
    ti = df["trial_index"].to_numpy()
    ok = np.diff(ti) == 1
    a = res[:-1][ok]
    b = res[1:][ok]
    if len(a) < 3 or a.std() == 0 or b.std() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(np.corrcoef(a, b)[0, 1])

results.name: recency_last_vs_second_example
results.description: For 3-4 example sets and non-example targets within 10 of some example, yes rate when the nearest example is the LAST shown minus when it is the SECOND shown; observed above null_mean means a recency advantage for the final example that the model (which only singles out the first example) fails to produce, below means the opposite.
results.code:
# name: recency_last_vs_second_example
# description: For 3-4 example sets and non-example targets within 10 of some example, yes rate when the nearest example is the LAST shown minus when it is the SECOND shown; observed above null_mean means a recency advantage for the final example that the model (which only singles out the first example) fails to produce, below means the opposite.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    ex = s.str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    n = (s.str.count(",") + 1).to_numpy()
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()[:, None]
    d = np.abs(ex - t)
    d = np.where(np.isnan(d), 1e9, d)
    dmin = d.min(axis=1)
    nearest = d.argmin(axis=1)
    ties = (d == dmin[:, None]).sum(axis=1) > 1
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    base = (n >= 3) & (dmin >= 1) & (dmin <= 10) & ~ties
    last = base & (nearest == n - 1)
    second = base & (nearest == 1)
    if last.sum() == 0 or second.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[last].mean() - r[second].mean())

results.name: single_minus_four_example_rate
results.description: Among non-example targets, yes rate after 1-example sets minus yes rate after 4-example sets; observed above null_mean means people narrow their generalization with more examples more strongly than the model (model's set-size effect too weak), below means the model over-narrows.
results.code:
# name: single_minus_four_example_rate
# description: Among non-example targets, yes rate after 1-example sets minus yes rate after 4-example sets; observed above null_mean means people narrow their generalization with more examples more strongly than the model (model's set-size effect too weak), below means the model over-narrows.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    ex = s.str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()[:, None]
    is_ex = (ex == t).any(axis=1)
    n = (s.str.count(",") + 1).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    a = (n == 1) & ~is_ex
    b = (n == 4) & ~is_ex
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: cell_unanimity_rate
results.description: Fraction of (number_set, target) cells with >=5 responses where all responses agree (all yes or all no); observed above null_mean means people respond more deterministically/consistently per stimulus than the model's graded p_yes predicts (model too noisy), below means the model is too deterministic.

results.name: trial_drift_slope
results.description: OLS slope (per 100 trials) of rating minus its (number_set, target)-cell mean on trial_index; nonzero observed vs null_mean means a drift in willingness to say yes over the session that the stationary model lacks (observed < null_mean: people become more conservative over time).
results.code:
# name: trial_drift_slope
# description: OLS slope (per 100 trials) of rating minus its (number_set, target)-cell mean on trial_index; nonzero observed vs null_mean means a drift in willingness to say yes over the session that the stationary model lacks (observed < null_mean: people become more conservative over time).
def test_statistic(df):
    r = df["rating"].astype(float)
    res = (r - r.groupby([df["number_set"], df["target"]]).transform("mean")).to_numpy()
    x = df["trial_index"].to_numpy().astype(float) / 100.0
    x = x - x.mean()
    den = (x * x).sum()
    if den == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float((x * res).sum() / den)

results.name: near_vs_far_gradient
results.description: Among non-example targets, yes rate for targets within 3 of the nearest example minus yes rate for targets 20+ away from every example; observed above null_mean means people show a steeper numeric-proximity (interval) generalization gradient than the model, below means a flatter one.
results.code:
# name: near_vs_far_gradient
# description: Among non-example targets, yes rate for targets within 3 of the nearest example minus yes rate for targets 20+ away from every example; observed above null_mean means people show a steeper numeric-proximity (interval) generalization gradient than the model, below means a flatter one.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()[:, None]
    dist = np.nanmin(np.abs(ex - t), axis=1)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    near = (dist >= 1) & (dist <= 3)
    far = dist >= 20
    if near.sum() == 0 or far.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[near].mean() - r[far].mean())

results.name: example_target_yes_rate
results.description: Yes rate on trials whose target is one of the shown examples; observed below null_mean means the model over-predicts endorsing the examples themselves (people are less at ceiling), above means it under-predicts.
